Learning Objectives
Describe the epidemiology and natural history of lumbar disk herniation.
Identify patient history and physical examination findings consistent with lumbar disk
herniation.
Describe neurologic findings associated with lumbar disk herniations depending on the level
and location of the herniation.
Describe nonsurgical treatment options and outcomes for lumbar disk herniations.
Describe surgical treatment options and outcomes for lumbar disk herniations.
Overview
Lumbar disk herniations (LDH) are common and can cause severe radicular pain and disability.

Most cases of radiculopathy caused by herniated disks resolve without management.
Nonsurgical management can alleviate symptoms as the herniated disk resorbs over time.
Microdiskectomy is highly effective at alleviating radicular pain and is associated with short-
and long-term outcomes that are better than those of nonsurgical management.

Overview
LDH is one of the most common conditions encountered by spine practitioners.
Although many disk herniations observed on imaging studies are asymptomatic, some
herniated disks may cause severe radicular pain, neurologic deficit, and disability. Most
cases of lumbar radiculopathy from LDH are self-limiting and resolve without
management.1 Nonsurgical management is helpful for alleviating symptoms as the
herniated disk resorbs. In patients in whom nonsurgical treatment fails to improve
symptoms or patients with a neurologic deficit, microdiskectomy is highly effective and is
associated with better short- and long-term outcomes than nonsurgical
management2 (Resource 1).
Epidemiology
Lifetime prevalence of symptomatic LDH is approximately 2%.
Peak incidence is in the fourth and fifth decades of life.
Most herniated disks are asymptomatic.
Approximately 10% of patients with symptomatic LDH undergo diskectomy.
Caudal segments are more commonly affected.

Epidemiology
LDH is very common, with approximately 40% of asymptomatic adult patients having a
herniated disk observed on a lumbar MRI.3 However, most herniated disks identified on
MRI are asymptomatic, and the lifetime prevalence of radiculopathy because of a LDH is
estimated to be approximately 2%.4 Given that most cases of radiculopathy from LDH

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004087
2/25

resolve spontaneously, only approximately 10% of patients with a symptomatic LDH
undergo diskectomy. The more caudal levels (L5-S1) are affected more commonly than
the more cranial levels (L1-L2), especially in younger patients. LDHs at the more cranial
levels tend to be found in older patients.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
The lumbar disk is composed of a well-hydrated, proteoglycan-rich nucleus pulposus
surrounded by a fibrous outer anulus fibrosus made of collagen fibrils.
The exiting nerve root (L4 nerve at the L4-L5 interspace) courses medially and caudally to the
pedicle and cranially to the disk space and then comes in contact with the disk in the foramen
and the far-lateral region. Therefore, the exiting nerve root can be compressed by foraminal
and far-lateral disk herniations (Figure 1).
The traversing nerve root (L5 nerve at the L4-L5 interspace) crosses the posterolateral portion
of the disk and can be compressed by paracentral disk herniations.
The cauda equina is contained within the thecal sac in the central portion of the canal and can
be compressed by a large central disk herniation.
Figure 1 Coronal (A) and axial (B) CT myelograms of the spine demonstrate the relative
positions of a lumbar disk herniation. A represents the central canal or central disk herniation.
B is the most common location and delineates a posterolateral disk herniation, C marks the

9/3/26, 3:56 PM
AAOS | Disk Herniations/Herniated Nucleus Pulposus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004087
3/25

zone of foraminal disk herniation, and D indicates the location of extraforaminal disk
herniation. (Reproduced from Chaudhary SB, Vives MJ: Lumbar and thoracic disk herniations,
in Grauer JN, ed: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update, ed 12. Rosemont, IL, American Academy of
Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2017, pp 591-599.)

Anatomy and Biomechanics
The lumbar disk is the largest avascular structure in the body. It is composed of a central
nucleus pulposus and contained by an anulus at its periphery. Blood vessels penetrate
the cartilaginous endplates and the outer anulus, and the inner anulus and nucleus
pulposus receive nutrition via diffusion. The nucleus pulposus is composed primarily of
proteoglycan and loosely arranged collagen fibers and serves to absorb axial load and
transmit those forces to the anulus. The anulus is made primarily of type I collagen fibers
oriented in concentric lamellae. These fibers can carry tensile loads and receive forces
transmitted to them by the nucleus. They also resist flexion, extension, rotation, and
axial bending.
The intervertebral disk is close to the exiting and traversing nerve roots. The exiting root
(L4 at the L4-L5 interspace) courses medially and caudally to the pedicle and cranially to
the disk space before coming into contact with the disk in the foramen and far-lateral
space. Therefore, the exiting root can be compressed by foraminal and far-lateral disk
herniations. The traversing nerve root (L5 at the L4-L5 interspace) crosses the
posterolateral portion of the disk in the lateral recess and is vulnerable to compression
by posterolateral and paracentral herniations. The cauda equina is located within the
thecal sac in the central portion of the canal and can be compressed by large central
herniations, which are the most common cause of cauda equina syndrome.
Etiology
Disk herniation is an early part of the degenerative disk cascade.
The posterolateral region of the disk is the weakest part of the anulus and the most common
region for disk herniation.

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004087
4/25

Most herniations occur without a specific inciting event; however, some herniations appear to
occur after increasing intradiscal pressure from lifting, sneezing, or performing a Valsalva
maneuver.
The herniated material may irritate the nerve root via mechanical compression and the strong
inflammatory response caused by the nuclear material.

Etiology
Disks degenerate as part of the aging process, with the nucleus pulposus becoming less
organized and more dehydrated, which results in disk height loss and increased load on
the anulus. The anulus can experience microtears and weakening, and the disk has
limited healing potential because of its poor blood supply. If the load transmitted to the
anulus by the nucleus exceeds its strength, it can rupture, and disk material, including
nucleus and cartilaginous endplate, can pass through the anular defect into the epidural
space. This material can irritate the nerve root via mechanical compression and by
generating a powerful inflammatory response. This, may result in pain, numbness, and
weakness.
Natural History
Radiculopathy caused by LDH resolves spontaneously in as many as 90% of patients within 3
months.
Pain tends to resolve most rapidly, with numbness and weakness improving more slowly and,
often, incompletely.

Natural History
The natural history of LDH is favorable, with as many of 90% of patients with LDH and
radiculopathy experiencing spontaneous resolution of symptoms within 3 months of
symptom onset.1 A study in which MRI was repeated after initial imaging studies
revealed LDH showed that the herniation was resorbed or shrank in most patients.5
Larger, extruded herniations tend to resorb faster and more completely than smaller

9/3/26, 3:56 PM
AAOS | Disk Herniations/Herniated Nucleus Pulposus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004087
5/25

protrusions. Pain is the first symptom to improve, with numbness and weakness taking
longer to improve. Frequently, these neurologic deficits do not completely resolve.
Risk Factors
Genetic factors likely play a role in predisposing patients to disk herniation and disk
degeneration; however, the molecular biology is not completely understood.
Obesity, smoking, heavy physical labor, and whole-body vibration also have been suggested as
risk factors for disk degeneration and herniation; however, the associations are relatively
weak.

Risk Factors
Lumbar disk degeneration and herniation are modestly associated with obesity,
smoking, heavy physical labor, and whole-body vibration; however, many patients with
LDH do not have known risk factors.6 Disk degeneration and herniation run in families,
and many genes have been implicated as risk factors for disk degeneration.7
Classification
MRI morphology and types of LDH (Figure 2)
Disk bulges involve more than 25% of the circumference of the disk and generally do not
cause considerable nerve compression.
Protrusions have the widest portion of the herniation at its base.
Extrusions have the widest portion of the herniation away from the base yet are still in
contact with the disk.
Sequestrations are fragments of herniated disk material that are no longer in contact with
the disk.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 3:56 PM
AAOS | Disk Herniations/Herniated Nucleus Pulposus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004087
6/25

Figure 2 Schematic drawing shows disk herniation location zones. In this image,
posterolateral, foraminal, and far-lateral herniations were combined as lateral herniations.
(Reproduced with permission from Pearson AM, Blood EA, Frymoyer JW, et al: SPORT lumbar
intervertebral disk herniation and back pain: Does treatment, location, or morphology matter?
Spine [Phila Pa 1976] 2008;33[4]:428-435.) Adapted from Spine 2006;26:E93-E113.)
Location (Figure 3)
Central disk herniations are located in the central portion of the canal and can compress the
thecal sac and, more rarely, nerve roots.
Paracentral herniations compress the traversing root in the lateral recess and are the most
common location for LDH.
Foraminal herniations are present between the pedicles and compress the exiting nerve
root.
Far-lateral herniations are located lateral to the pedicle and compress the exiting nerve root.

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004087
7/25

Figure 3 Schematic drawing shows disk herniation morphologies. In this image, extrusions and
sequestrations were combined as extrusions/sequestrations. (Adapted with permission from
Fardon DF, Milette PC: Nomenclature and classification of lumbar disc pathology:
Recommendations of the Combined task Forces of the North American Spine Society,
American Society of Spine Radiology, and American Society of Neuroradiology. Spine [Phila Pa
1976] 2006;26[5]:E93-E113.)

Classification
LDHs can be classified according to morphology observed on MRI.8 Disk bulges tend to
be broad-based asymmetries in the disk that involve more than 25% of the
circumference of the disk and do not cause considerable nerve compression. Disk
protrusions have the widest portion of the herniation at their base. Extrusions have the
widest portion of the herniation away from the base and are still in contact with the disk.
Sequestrations are herniated fragments no longer in contact with the disk.
Herniations also can be classified according to location. Central and paracentral
herniations are located in the central portion of the canal and can compress the thecal
sac and the traversing roots. Posterolateral herniations, the most common location type,
are located in the lateral recess and compress the traversing root. Foraminal herniations
are located between the cranial and caudal pedicles and compress the exiting root. Far-

9/3/26, 3:56 PM
AAOS | Disk Herniations/Herniated Nucleus Pulposus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004087
8/25

lateral herniations are located lateral to the lateral border of the pedicle and also
compress the exiting root.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
The patient typically presents with varying degrees of back and leg pain.
Some patients report a prodrome of back pain followed by more severe leg pain.
Radicular pain follows the dermatomal path of the affected root and may be accompanied by
motor or sensory deficits.
Cauda equina syndrome is rare and involves lower extremity motor weakness and sensory
deficits, saddle anesthesia, and bladder and bowel dysfunction.

Patient History
Some patients with LDH report an acute onset of symptoms after an inciting event, such
as lifting or sneezing; however, no inciting event is identified in most patients. The typical
presentation is back pain radiating to a unilateral lower extremity in a dermatomal
pattern that can be associated with weakness and/or numbness. Some patients report a
prodrome of back pain followed by the development of more severe leg pain. Sitting,
forward flexion, and lifting tend to exacerbate symptoms.
Cauda equina syndrome is a relatively rare presentation, usually caused by a large
central herniation that compresses the entire cauda equina. The syndrome includes
bilateral lower extremity pain, weakness, and numbness, as well as saddle anesthesia
and bowel and bladder dysfunction. Bladder dysfunction most often manifests as
urinary retention. Urinary retention is an essential component of the diagnosis. Urinary
incontinence typically is a late finding and manifests as an overflow incontinence.
Physical Examination
SEND FEEDBACK

AAOS | Disk Herniations/Herniated Nucleus Pulposus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004087
9/25

Lumbar flexion typically is limited more than extension; however, both may be affected.
Pain with the straight leg raise test results from increased nerve root tension and a lack of
normal excursion of the root at the herniation site. The ipsilateral straight leg raise test is
sensitive for LDH; however, the crossed straight leg raise test (raising the leg contralateral to
the symptoms) is more specific.
For upper lumbar radiculopathy (L2-L3), the femoral nerve tension test can be used as a
provocative test. A positive test re-creates pain in the anterior thigh.
A thorough neurologic examination is essential. Herniated disks usually affect a specific nerve
root, resulting in pain and numbness in a specific dermatome, weakness in a specific
myotome, and characteristic reflex losses (Table 1).
If cauda equina syndrome is expected, a rectal examination is important to evaluate and
document anal sphincter function and perianal sensation.

Physical Examination
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 3:56 PM
AAOS | Disk Herniations/Herniated Nucleus Pulposus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004087
10/25

The physical examination is an essential aspect of diagnosing lumbar radiculopathy
caused by LDH. With acute radiculopathy caused by LDH, lumbar flexion is limited more
than lumbar extension. Patients also may have tenderness in the sciatic notch. Straight
leg raising between 30° and 70° increases stretch on the sciatic nerve and the lower
lumbar nerve roots (L4 through S1). The ipsilateral straight leg raise test is a sensitive
test for radiculopathy caused by LDH; however, it is less specific. In the crossed straight
leg raise test, a straight leg raise is performed with the leg contralateral to the radicular
pain. This test is less sensitive but more specific than the ipsilateral straight leg raise test.
For upper lumbar root pathology (L2-L3), the femoral tension test can be performed to
stretch the femoral nerve and the upper lumbar roots. A positive test re-creates pain in
the anterior thigh. A thorough neurologic examination, focusing on each of the lumbar
roots, is essential to localize the involved level. Frequently, abnormal radiographic
findings are observed at multiple levels, and diagnosis of the involved level based on the
patient history and the physical examination will focus the interpretation of MRIs and
improved diagnostic accuracy. Each of the lumbar roots is associated with a specific
dermatome and myotome, and dysfunction of some roots may cause diminished
reflexes.
If cauda equina syndrome is expected, a rectal examination is important to assess and
document anal sphincter tone and function and perirectal sensation. Post-void bladder
scanning (preferably via catheterization) should be performed and frequently will reveal
a high volume of urine (200 mL) retained in the bladder. Dysfunction of the sacral nerve
roots typically results in urinary retention and subsequent overflow incontinence.
Imaging Studies
Plain radiographs frequently are normal or show degenerative changes. They may be helpful
to obtain preoperatively to help plan level localization, especially in patients with transitional
lumbosacral anatomy.
MRI is the preferred imaging modality for the evaluation of LDH. This imaging modality allows
for high-quality imaging of disk material and the lumbar nerve roots (Figure 4).

If concern for re-herniation exists postoperatively, the addition of contrast to T1-weighted MRI
allows surgeons to distinguish scarring (enhances with contrast) from disk material (does not
enhance with contrast).
Patients with contraindications to MRI can undergo CT myelography to allow for better
visualization of the nerve roots than observed with standard CT.
Figure 4 MRIs show the variability of disk herniation morphology. T2-weighted MRI is the best
imaging modality to diagnose and identify the disk type. A, Axial T2-weighted MRI of a spine
shows an L5-S1 disk protrusion. Sagittal (B) and axial (C) T2-weighted MRIs of a spine show a
lumbar disk extrusion. (Reproduced from Chaudhary SB, Vives MJ: Lumbar and thoracic disk
herniations, in Grauer JN, ed: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update, ed 12. Rosemont, IL, American
Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2017, pp 591-599.)

Imaging Studies
If LDH is suspected based on the patient history and physical examination, MRI is the
preferred imaging modality. This imaging modality allows for high-quality imaging of the
nerve roots and disk material. On T2-weighted MRIs, herniated disk material usually
appears as a low intensity signal (black), whereas the cerebrospinal fluid surrounding the
nerve roots in the thecal sac appear as a high intensity signal (white). This allows for
good visualization of the herniated disk and evaluation of the degree of nerve root and
thecal sac compression.
If patients have undergone a prior diskectomy, postcontrast T1-weighted MRIs also
should be obtained because disk and scar tissue both appear as low intensity signal on
T2-weighted MRIs. On postcontrast T1-weighted MRIs, vascularized scarring will enhance

AAOS | Disk Herniations/Herniated Nucleus Pulposus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004087
12/25

with contrast, whereas avascular disk material does not enhance. In patients in whom
MRI is contraindicated, CT myelography allows for visualization of the nerve roots and
evaluation for nerve root and thecal sac compression. This imaging modality provides
limited evaluation of foraminal and far-lateral disk herniations because the intrathecal
contrast does not extend into these regions.
Plain radiographs do not allow for visualization of disk material or nerve roots; therefore,
they do not play a role in the diagnosis of LDH; however, they should be obtained
preoperatively for planning level localization, especially in patients with transitional
lumbosacral anatomy.
Diagnosis
Diagnosis of radiculopathy caused by LDH is a result of combining data obtained from the
patient history, physical examination, and MRIs.

Diagnosis
Diagnosing radiculopathy caused by LDH requires combining data from the patient
history, physical examination, and MRIs. None of the elements on their own are
sufficiently sensitive or specific to allow for accurate diagnosis, and clinical acumen is
required to determine if a disk herniation observed on MRI is the source of a patient’s
symptoms. Approximately 40% of asymptomatic adults have MRIs that show LDH;
therefore, another cause of pain is present in some patients with leg pain and an MRI
showing a herniated disk.3 The clinician must confirm that the location of the pain and
any findings of the neurologic examination are consistent with the findings observed on
MRI. In patients with radicular symptoms in whom the diagnosis is unclear, additional
neurologic evaluation, including electromyography and nerve conduction studies, should
be considered.
Differential Diagnosis

9/3/26, 3:56 PM
AAOS | Disk Herniations/Herniated Nucleus Pulposus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004087
13/25

Spinal stenosis, facet cyst, tumor, sacroiliac dysfunction, piriformis syndrome, peripheral
neuropathy, lumbar plexopathy, and epidural abscess may cause symptoms that overlap with
lumbar radiculopathy caused by LDH.

Differential Diagnosis
The differential diagnosis for lumbar radiculopathy is broad and includes other
degenerative pathologies, such as spinal stenosis and facet cyst. Other compressive
lesions, such as tumor or infection, also can cause radiculopathy; however, these
frequently are accompanied by red-flag symptoms, such as weight loss, fevers, and
systemic illness. Any peripheral nerve lesion also can cause radicular symptoms, such as
lumbar plexopathy, piriformis syndrome, or peripheral neuropathy. A thorough patient
history and physical examination usually can rule out infection or tumor, and MRI will
demonstrate other spinal sources of nerve compression. In patients in whom MRI is
normal yet radicular symptoms are present, referral to neurology and consideration of
electrodiagnostic studies is appropriate.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Patients with acute (less than 4 to 6 weeks) lumbar radiculopathy should initially undergo
nonsurgical treatment.
Physical therapy is a first-line treatment option. No one approach to physical therapy has been
shown to be superior, and an individualized program guided by a physical therapist is
recommended.
NSAIDs are the first-line medical treatment option.
Lumbar epidural steroid injection affords short-term pain improvement but does not decrease
the risk for surgical management in the longer term.9,10

Nonsurgical Management
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 3:56 PM
AAOS | Disk Herniations/Herniated Nucleus Pulposus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004087
14/25

Patients with acute (less than 6 weeks) lumbar radiculopathy without progressive
weakness should initially undergo nonsurgical treatment. First-line treatment consists of
physical therapy and NSAIDs. Multiple physical therapy approaches have been
advocated, without any technique being shown to be superior. Some patients have a
preference for physical therapy exercises, and individualized treatment programs guided
by a physical therapist are recommended. A short course of oral steroids may be
considered in patients who do not respond to NSAIDs. Opioid pain medications are best
avoided because of their poor adverse-effect profile and risk of dependence. They
frequently are ineffective for radicular pain. Gabapentin frequently is used, without
much evidence supporting its use. Lumbar epidural steroid injection via a transforaminal
or intralaminar approach affords short-term pain relief but likely does not change the
longer-term risk for surgical management.9,10
Surgical Management
Indications
Patients with radiculopathy caused by LDH who have had symptoms for more 6 weeks and
who have failed to improve sufficiently despite nonsurgical treatment should be considered
candidates for surgical treatment.
Patients with LDH and progressive motor weakness should strongly consider surgical
treatment.
Cauda equina syndrome is an absolute indication for urgent surgical management.

Indications
Surgical management is indicated for LDH in patients with radiculopathy that has
persisted for at least 6 weeks and who have failed to improve sufficiently despite a trial
of nonsurgical treatment. Delayed surgical management for at least 6 weeks is standard
practice because of the high rate of spontaneous improvement during this time frame.
Surgical treatment should be considered elective in patients without a substantial
neurologic deficit, and a shared decision-making process should be used. Patients with
considerable motor weakness, especially progressive motor weakness, should strongly

9/3/26, 3:56 PM
AAOS | Disk Herniations/Herniated Nucleus Pulposus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004087
15/25

consider surgical treatment. Cauda equina syndrome is an absolute indication for urgent
surgical management.
Patients without a considerable neurologic deficit who have had symptoms for less than
6 weeks should not undergo surgical treatment because spontaneous resolution is likely
to occur. If symptoms have resolved but a herniated disk is observed on MRI, then
patients should not undergo surgical treatment because their symptoms likely will not
recur. Major medical comorbidities that preclude safe anesthesia also are
contraindications to surgical management.
Techniques/Procedures
Limited diskectomy is favored over complete diskectomy because it results in less back pain.11
Open microdiskectomy results in outcomes similar to those achieved via tubular
diskectomy.12
Percutaneous endoscopic microdiskectomy has been adopted by some surgeons; however, it
has not been rigorously evaluated, and indications remain unclear.

Techniques/Procedures
Traditionally, surgeons would perform a complete diskectomy after removing the
herniation. Although this reduced the risk of re-herniation, it resulted in considerably
worse low back pain.11 The current standard of care is limited microdiskectomy, in which
only the herniated fragment and any superficial free fragments are removed (Resource
2). A high-quality randomized controlled trial was performed to compare the outcomes
of open microdiskectomy and tubular microdiskectomy and reported similar results
between the two groups.12 Percutaneous endoscopic microdiskectomy has not been
widely adopted. Percutaneous endoscopic microdiskectomy has not been rigorously
evaluated, and indications for it remain unclear.
Patient Positioning

AAOS | Disk Herniations/Herniated Nucleus Pulposus

The patient should be positioned to keep the lumbar spine in a flexed posture to open the
spinal canal.
Options include an Andrews frame in the knees-to-chest position, a Wilson frame, and a
Jackson table with a sling.

Patient Positioning
All patient positioning options share the same goal of keeping the patient’s lumbar spine
flexed, which opens the spinal canal and makes the surgical procedure technically easier,
requiring less bony resection. An Andrews frame, a Wilson frame, and a Jackson table
with the knees in a sling all accomplish this goal.
Surgical Approaches
Midline incision with unilateral laminotomy for posterolateral and paracentral herniations
Wiltse (transpedicular) approach between the multifidus and longissimus to access far-lateral
disk herniations (Figure 5)
Large central herniations frequently require laminectomy.

Figure 5 Drawing shows the extraforaminal approach for far-lateral disks. The isolated
extraforaminal exposure for a far-lateral disk, shown on the left side at the L4-L5 level in this
image, requires minimal removal of the superolateral aspect of the L4-L5 facet joint (triple
arrows). After resecting the intertransversarious ligament, muscle, and fascia, the L4 root is
directly exposed in the far-lateral compartment (NR). With this exposure, the far-lateral
sequestrated fragment may be removed (double large arrows); however, no medial access to
disk excision or decompression of stenosis is provided. (Reproduced with permission from
Epstein NE: Different surgical approaches to far lateral lumbar disc herniations. J Spinal Disord
1995;8[5]:383-394.)

Surgical Approaches
The midline approach with a laminotomy allows access to posterolateral and paracentral
herniations. A Wiltse approach between the multifidus and longissimus muscles allows
for a transpedicular approach to access far-lateral herniations.13 Foraminal herniations
can be accessed via either approach and occasionally require a complete facetectomy
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 3:56 PM
AAOS | Disk Herniations/Herniated Nucleus Pulposus
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004087
18/25

and fusion. Large central herniations, often encountered in patients with cauda equina
syndrome, usually require a midline laminectomy to safely remove the disk.
Postoperative Management
Surgical management frequently is performed as a same-day procedure.
Debate exists about postoperative activity restrictions, with some studies indicating no benefit
from postoperative restrictions.14,15

Postoperative Management
Currently, most lumbar microdiskectomies are performed as outpatient surgical
procedures. Appropriate multimodal analgesia is essential for successful outpatient
diskectomy. Many surgeons employ postoperative activity restrictions, believing that this
reduces the risk of re-herniation. Some literature suggests that such restrictions do not
reduce re-herniation rates and result in a slower return to regular activity and work.14 In
a randomized trial, Bono et al15 reported equivalent clinical outcomes, irrespective of
the length of postoperative restrictions.
Complications
Durotomy: less than 5%
Infection: less than 2%
Nerve root injury: approximately 1 in 500

Complications
Serious complications after lumbar diskectomy are rare. Patients with re-herniation
typically present with symptoms similar to those experienced with their initial herniation.
Incidental durotomy (eg, dural tear) is less common with diskectomy than with surgical
management for spinal stenosis and occurs in fewer than 5% of patients. MostSEND FEEDBACK

Outcomes
Patients can improve with nonsurgical and surgical treatment.
Surgical management results in faster and more complete improvement than nonsurgical
management.
The advantage of surgical management relative to nonsurgical management decreases with
time.
Patients with symptom duration longer than 6 to 9 months may improve less with surgical
management than those who undergo surgical management closer to symptom onset.
Patients undergoing revision diskectomy improve; however, the improvement is less than that
with primary surgical management, and the complication rate is higher.
Most patients who undergo surgical management for cauda equina syndrome report
improvement in bowel, bladder, and sexual function postoperatively; however, 25% to 50% of
patients have a residual neurologic deficit.
Surgical management for cauda equina syndrome performed within 48 hours of symptom
onset is associated with better neurologic outcomes than more delayed surgical management.

Outcomes
Many large, prospective studies have compared surgical and nonsurgical outcomes for
LDH.2,16-22 These studies have shown that patients treated nonsurgically and surgically
improve substantially from baseline; however, patients treated surgically improve faster
and have better patient-reported outcomes. A recent randomized trial demonstrated
superior resolution of pain intensity in patients treated surgically.23 In some patients,
this difference is durable at 10 years postoperatively. The advantage of surgical
management over nonsurgical management persists but diminishes with time.

Prolonged duration of symptoms may compromise the outcome of surgical
management and lead to chronic deficits and persistent pain. An exact threshold has not
been established; however, many studies suggest that delaying surgical management for
more than 6 to 9 months after symptom onset is associated with poorer patient-
reported outcomes.24,25 However, even in patients with symptom duration for more
than 6 months, surgical management still results in better outcomes than nonsurgical
management.
Patients are at risk of recurrent disk herniation, even after successful surgical or
nonsurgical management. Recurrent herniation occurs in approximately 10% of patients
within 8 years of treatment.2
Revision diskectomy results in symptom improvement; however, the magnitude of
improvement is less than that with primary surgical management and the complication
rate is higher. Patients undergoing surgical treatment for cauda equina syndrome have
improved function; however, 25% to 50% of patients have residual neurologic deficits
postoperatively. Surgical management performed within 48 hours of symptom onset is
associated with better neurologic function than more delayed surgical management.
Whether emergent surgical management (within 12 hours of symptom onset) leads to
better outcomes remains unclear.
